analysis.one_liner: Bans former fossil fuel executives and lobbyists from top energy and environment posts for 10 years.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one senator with zero cosponsors, was referred to committee and never received a markup, vote, or floor action before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar anyone who spent the previous 10 years as a fossil fuel company executive, a lobbyist for the fossil fuel industry, or an employee of a fossil fuel trade association from serving as a department head in a long list of top posts — including Secretary of Energy, EPA Administrator, Secretary of the Interior, and Chief of Staff to the President — or as a political appointee at the agencies that regulate energy and the environment [S2][S3]. The idea is to keep the people who run the oil, gas, and coal industries from then writing the rules that govern those same industries [S2][S3]. The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or any action after being referred to committee [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who breathe the air, pay energy bills, and depend on environmental and energy regulators to act independently. The bill would also protect the integrity of agencies like EPA, Interior, and Energy by keeping the revolving door — moving between industry and the government that regulates it — closed at the top [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who relies on independent regulators

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits anyone who served in the previous 10 years as a fossil fuel executive, fossil fuel lobbyist, or fossil fuel trade association employee from being appointed to roughly 19 covered posts, including Secretary of Energy, Secretary of the Interior, EPA Administrator, Secretary of State, and Chief of Staff to the President, or serving in those roles in an acting capacity [S2][S3].

Extends the ban to all political appointees at the Interior Department, EPA, Energy Department, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, NOAA, the Council on Environmental Quality, the Office of Science and Technology Policy, and the Office of Management and Budget — the agencies that directly regulate fossil fuels and set climate policy [S2][S3].

Carves out an exception for employees whose work was principally in wind, solar, or other renewable energy divisions, so the ban targets fossil fuel extraction and production rather than clean-energy expertise [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel companies, their lobbying firms, and trade associations would lose their most direct channel into top government posts. People with recent fossil fuel industry experience would be ineligible for those jobs even if otherwise qualified [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, gas, and coal companies and lobbyists

drawbacks.text: A flat 10-year ban would exclude some people with genuine and relevant energy expertise, including career energy professionals who have worked inside oil and gas companies in technical or policy roles, regardless of their individual qualifications [S3].

The ban is drawn by industry type, not conduct: it would bar a former fossil fuel executive who later became a clean-energy advocate, while a former official from a bank that finances fossil fuels would not be covered, because the definition covers entities that extract or produce fossil fuel, not those that finance them [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill addresses a symptom rather than the whole revolving door: it covers a defined list of posts and agencies and leaves other influential roles, such as senior White House advisers outside the covered list, untouched [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — keeping recent fossil fuel industry insiders out of the top jobs that regulate them — is real and directly addresses a documented pattern in recent administrations. The costs are modest and mostly about over-breadth: some qualified energy professionals would be excluded, and the carve-out definitions leave edge cases. On balance, a straightforward ethics rule whose main downside is bluntness.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the BIG OIL Cabinet Act in the Senate on November 21, 2019 [S1][S2].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors, from either party [S4].

After being read twice, it was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which is the last action ever taken on it — no hearing, markup, vote, or floor action followed [S5].
The bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and all legislation not passed dies at that point.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel companies and their lobbying firms kept the door open to top energy and environment posts; no one pushed the bill forward beyond a single sponsor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies and their lobbyists

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on November 21, 2019; it was his proposal and no senator joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: Ron Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; bills do not reach the floor without the majority leader's scheduling, and this one never left committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls show how support split; the only recorded action was its Democratic sponsor's introduction, with zero cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.note: The bill would bar their executives and lobbyists from the very cabinet and agency posts that regulate them, cutting off their most direct route to influence over energy and environmental policy. That influence channel is precisely what runs against ordinary people's interest in independent regulation [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Fossil fuel lobbying firms and trade associations
industries.note: Registered fossil fuel lobbyists and trade association employees would become ineligible for the covered posts for 10 years after leaving, reducing the market value of their revolving-door connections [S2][S3].
